Name: 0_farmer_dear_joyful_spirit
Representative_Docs:
['Oh, what has happened to me,
On my last journey that I took,
Every person would shudder at it,
If I shared the story with him:
They had barely set sail,
Three days out at sea,
When a storm on the waves,
Broke the great mast in two;
The ship was rising, the ship was falling;
Finally it got such a blow,
That it ran aground on a rock,
And broke into a thousand pieces.
Then it was time for men to save themselves,
Swimming was the very best:
I had to move like a duck,
Disturbed in its nest:
But when I was swimming in the water,
Ah, I will never forget,
That almost a shark with its snout,
Bit me in the arm:
I swam all the way to the shore,
And thus escaped danger;
Soon I climbed ashore,
And walked on up to here.
What shall I do now,
Wet and cold in this state,
Sickly and bruised inside:
Ah, how do I get off this street:
If the innkeeper now would vouch,
And tap on credit,
Then I would be free of worries,
And I think of no sorrow;
Although I have no money for this,
I have spent my coins there,
I bet he will not be so angry,
That he won’t give credit now.
I have not yet lost courage:
That spirit is alive,
Said the innkeeper might hear it,
Who certainly sang the babok song,
If you want to leave here right away,
Or I will cover you on your lap,
With a broomstick,
So you will look like no human:
There is the woman who is much softer,
She has blood running from my nose,
I bet she calls me soon behind,
There she already gives the signal.
Well friend, what is your desire,
Well friend, what is your desire,
Make me say it quickly;
Because the people inside are waiting for me there,
Also I don’t have much time, my father,
Why do you look so sad and sour,
Come, just tell me.
Well, how now Miss Griet,
Well, how now Miss Griet,
Have you forgotten me so,
Tell me honestly, don’t you know me,
I am your old customer Piet,
Who spent and lent a lot of money here.
You, Piet, I have never seen,
You, Piet, I have never seen,
So poor and so poor;
I praise your money and goods,
Wasted, you’ll be punished if you do more,
Therefore just go from here quietly,
You naked louse.
Well Griet, what talk is that,
Well Griet, what talk is that,
Is it serious or is it madness:
I say that I do not want to go from here,
Before I speak your man or boy,
Go tap a jug of old beer immediately,
And call her here.
Well scoundrel, now I don’t want to,
Well scoundrel, now I don’t want to,
Call my man or boy,
You will not come into my house,
I see you have neither coin nor cross,
Therefore make no noise here:
Away naked louse.
Don’t be so hasty,
Don’t be so hasty,
I will tell you my story:
But she has gone on very angrily,
And left me standing here on the street;
But who comes there in rich attire,
Ah, it is my mate.
His mate gives him money, and they go together
To the inn, where Piet was then welcome,
And sang with a glass of wine the conclusion.
Let us be merry,
With the girls and the fresh wine;
Hey, quickly grab the glass,
Drink cheerfully, let the wine go down,
Come pour again,
And let us toast with joy in mind.', "How long that journey also takes;
It is now the fourth year;
How sadly fearful that time falls upon me!
I took an East Indies sailor,
A sea dog, fresh, healthy, and strong,
Greatly loved by the ship's crew,
Also by his Officers, as I notice:
A man like a child.

Thoroughly learned in ship work,
A truly experienced man:
Who neither fights, nor swears, nor drinks, nor curses,
Who can speak fiercely
When it is necessary, and otherwise not.
Oh, if I could see him again,
There would be an end to my sorrow;
How welcome he was!
Look, whether I say it or stay silent
I am very uneasy,
Because I get no word or answer...
Who knows on which coast
The ship has come to grief! Perhaps
It perished with man and mouse...
Oh Bram, shall I never see you again?
Won't you come home to your wife!

Who knows where he travels and wanders!
Whether he suffers from hunger!
And is sick and sighing, even dying.
I may have already lost him.
It is already far beyond the year
Since I last saw his spirit;
I sat with the child, and he stood there,
By bright clear day.
He looked quite well,
So handsome, so well made:
It is certain that this means something good;
He looked earnestly at the child.
There he stood, in his long trousers,
No six feet from me;
I saw very clearly the silk cloth
That I had given him as a gift:

Naturally, tied around his neck.
How immensely happy I was!
I had long hoped for this sight.
I thought, he is thinking of me.
My Bram was never a frivolous fellow,
Says everyone who knows him.
He has a valuable intellect;
Oh, he is such a good man!
I got this child when he was still
Less than eight weeks at sea.
He was well-made in body and limb,
It went well with him.
People suspected I served for Min
Regarding that:
But I had no intention of that,
I declined the Lady.

I give my child what God gave me
For the little blood.
I also promised it to my husband, and he
Left me on this.
Come to mother, sweet Jan;
Oh, if your daddy were here!
If he saw you, I know the man
Would cry with joy.
Yes, if you only knew, my dear Bram,
How day and night,
I cared for our little lamb;
How I fulfilled my duty!
He left my sight not once;
I earned my bread with the needle.
I feared gossip more
Than the pale death.

But why do I torment myself so
And worry, and sigh, and cry.
The man probably has it well;
I can, after little time,
See him again, healthy and fresh.
That would be a joy!
‘Then it’s a new fair again’:
So says my neighbor Styn.
And see, she already knows this of old;
That I can well guess:
Sailors always have good wives,
That is all we do.
They visit us so cheerfully,
They don’t look stern or angry:
Hear, it doesn’t grieve me that for myself
I chose a handsome sailor girl.

What is the noise in the street?
It is already flying towards Westdyk...
It’s as if guns are firing too!
I’ll go and look as well;
So I get the right information;
Come with me, mother, Jan.
There lies the ship; look, Jantje, there.
Oh Lord, there stands my husband.", '1.
Friends come all together,
And listen to my song:
I have no reason to be ashamed,
That I am going to sing this:
It is how I sharpen scissors and knives,
For all people and cares,
Tiereliere, Tierela,
My stone turns left and right,
By stirring all of my leg.

2.
As long as my stone can sharpen,
So I earn pennies and shillings;
I hear no children whine,
From hunger in my house:
They have no discomfort,
Always going with the beggar's bag,
Tiereliere, etc.

3.
I take it all with thanks,
That comes here by chance,
Even if it is just a penny,
That I will earn:
Two pennies for a rusty knife,
An elle* is also a penny,
Tiereliere, etc.

(*an elle is a Dutch unit of length)

4.
Let the weavers keep weaving,
Until they become weak,
It is a lot for those who can give,
Twelve stuivers to his wife;
I earn with my grinding stone,
Often in just one hour,
Tiereliere, etc.

5.
The smith must work hard,
Continuously at the fire,
He may not strengthen it,
With a pot of beer;
Because of their small gain,
But I often play in there,
Tiereliere, etc.

6.
The miller who winnows much,
But receives it with his shovel,
The baker can also steal,
Because he also keeps a pinch:
But I with my grinding stone said,
Earn money always in fairness,
Tiereliere, etc.

7.
The tailor makes a show,
Already for ten stuivers a day,
When winter is at the door,
Then he almost cracks,
I do not fear the winter,
Provided everyone offers me something to sharpen,
Tiereliere, etc.

8.
The shoemakers storm,
Already for a small gain,
Beat on their awl and lasts,
They still have the curls in it;
Must I from the beginning of the week,
With my wagon on the route,
Tiereliere, etc.

9.
I know there is still a pair of scissors,
That must be sharpened,
At the house of my strings,
That is already profit for me;
Then I go home with pleasure,
And go drink a jug of beer,
Tiereliere, etc.

10.
Ship carpenters boys,
Your work now goes well,
Through the swinging and little sleeping,
You make many a strong man;
Although I also kiss the girl,
My stone still turns on its time,
Tiereliere, etc.

11.
House carpenters belong,
Under St. Joseph’s Guild,
Your work can please much,
But you would not have wished;
That you could sharpen scissors,
I know that you never walked empty,
Tiereliere, etc.

12.
The masons, you know,
They lay much on the roof,
The foreman looks through a toy,
But then Jan gets the sack:
Yet I look no one in the eye;
I am my own boss and guardian,
Tiereliere, etc.

13.
The printers' loose spirits,
They print all that is much,
Most of what they earn,
They drink it down their throat;
Because many wear patch upon patch,
Where I am always equally skilled,
Tiereliere, etc.

14.
Surgeons are seen walking,
Scraping many beards,
They could buy no bread,
If I were not there,
Because I must sharpen their fine knives,
Lancets big and small,
Tiereliere, etc.

15.
For do you think of the hairdressers,
They seem great gentlemen,
But if you don't count the show,
It is all for the bread:
They cut the ladies nicely in the hair,
But mostly decency makes the scissors,
Tiereliere, etc.

16.
The butchers great balls,
When they are in the hall,
Most they may fool around,
But that is all;
Because I do not sharpen their knives finely,
How would they then get the beast small?
Tiereliere, etc.

17.
The seamstresses go out sewing,
And that for small money,
To make jackets, cabayes*,
Or otherwise something fixed;
But if I did not sharpen the scissors sharp,
They would never be ready among the people,
Tiereliere, etc.

(*cabaye is probably a type of garment)

18.
I also sharpen my little knife,
Already with a dear girl,
Who likes a little chat,
But only in silence;
They also like me to do it so,
And do it carefully with decency,
Tiereliere, etc.

19.
Diamond grinders light workers,
What do you think of those,
They grind diamonds,
And that also with a stone,
But the girl goes with the gain,
Where I feed my bee as I please,
Tiereliere, etc.

20.
The song singers walk,
And that from March to March,
To sell songs,
And scream like a hart*;
For small gain remain in the city,
I call scissors sharpening, then I win something,
Tiereliere, etc.

(*hart means "deer" but likely "heart" is intended here)

21.
I say for the last,
Many trades are good,
But mine is the very best,
Although I often must:
Sleep in hay and straw in the stable,
I have the livelihood for nothing,
Tiereliere, etc.']

would you give something in my little shoe, God will reward you then.

I love Saint Nicholas.

put on your best robe  
and ride along to Spain,  
bring little apples from Oranges,

give the little children something.  

Saint Nicholas, that good lord,  
comes back every year,  
with his little horses in front of his wagon,

searching diligently for knowledge,

your soul, a temple of the Holy Spirit,

your body waged a heavy war,  
so that it would remain under the spirit.

After you were consecrated a priest,
you further cultivated virtue,
your body waged a heavy war,
so that it would be more subject to the spirit.

6.
You slept and ate much less than before,
and your drink was only clear water,
your clothes were poor, yet neat,
the spirit always concerned in prayer.

7.
When both your parents were dead,
you inherited a very great treasure from them,
which you neither wasted uselessly
nor locked up in an iron chest.

8.
You gave to the poor generously their share,
for you did not keep it as your own,
but as steward appointed by the Lord,
thereby also this deed of yours is told:

9.
In Patara was a poor nobleman,
who had three beautiful daughters by his wife;
but now that they had grown old,
he could no longer maintain them.

10.
So he gave them advice,
which was deadly bad for their souls,
that for a piece of money they would soil their purity
with dishonorableness.

11.
As soon as Saint Nicholas understood this,
he went by night to the same house,
threw through the window a bag of gold,
by which one daughter was saved.

12.
Once again he returned at home,
and threw the gold once more through the window;
through this the second daughter was married,
so great power had this hidden gold.

13.
The third daughter he remembered,
and at night brought the money into the house,
by which he preserved her body in distress
and her soul from death.

14.
O wise and merciful prelate,
you know our slippery state,
through which our thoughtless young youth
is quickly carried away from their innocent virtue.

15.
Grant us from God a devout mind,
that always purely does His will;
give us the gold of love in our shoe,
so that we avoid the punishment of God’s rod.

For him, of money or sweet food,
the night before the festival he stayed awake:
there is some sugar in it,
some money, some strawberries, more or less,
according to what was lived by
father’s and mother’s will before:
for if it has shorn the beast too hard,
and has been too bad,
Saint Nicholas will put in his shoe,
instead of money, a piece of coal.']
